text: Everything in this chapter so far — the Security log, the specific Event IDs, even what Sysmon adds on top — depends on audit policy being configured to generate those events in the first place. Audit policy lives in Local Security Policy, or in a domain, Group Policy, under Advanced Audit Policy Configuration. Without the right subcategory enabled, the event you're hunting for in Event Viewer was simply never written.

Advanced audit policy breaks into categories. Logon/Logoff governs 4624 and 4625 from Lesson 10. Account Management governs 4720 and 4728, also from Lesson 10. Privilege Use governs events like 4672. Object Access governs auditing of specific files or registry keys, but only once a matching SACL is also set on that object. Policy Change governs changes to the audit policy itself — so an attacker trying to quietly weaken logging generates an event of their own.

auditpol.exe checks and sets audit policy from the command line — useful for scripting a baseline across many machines, or confirming what's enabled on a system you're investigating, without opening a single console window.

Logging everything sounds safer, but it isn't free. Enabling every subcategory, especially Object Access across a busy file server, can generate an overwhelming volume of events — storage and SIEM cost climbs fast, and the handful of events that actually matter get harder to find, not easier. That's alert fatigue. Logging too little is the opposite failure: if Account Management auditing was never enabled, 4720 and 4728 simply don't exist on that machine, no matter how good your detection logic is.

The right answer is neither extreme — it's enabling the categories that map to detections your team will actually use, at a volume your storage and SIEM can absorb. Logon/Logoff and Account Management are cheap and nearly always worth it; Object Access is powerful but expensive, so it's scoped to a handful of genuinely sensitive files, not an entire file server. Chapter 4 moves to Linux, starting with sudo and the sudoers file in depth.
